chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Khalid, from some of our companions, from Ali ibn Uqba ibn Qays ibn Sim'an ibn Abi Rubayha — the freed slave of the Messenger of God (may God's blessings be upon him and his family) — said:

The Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) was asked: 'By what did you recognize your Lord?' He said: 'By that which He Himself made known to me.' It was said: 'And how did He make Himself known to you?' He said: 'No image resembles Him, nor can He be perceived by the senses, nor can He be compared with people.'

He is Near in His remoteness and Remote in His nearness. He is above every thing, and it cannot be said that anything is above Him. He is before every thing, and it cannot be said that He has a before. He is within things, not like a thing that enters into another thing; and He is outside of things, not like a thing that exits from another thing.
Glory be to the One Who is like this, and nothing else is like this. And for every thing there is an Initiator.

key_terms.سُبْحَانَ: Glory/Praise (subhan) — liturgical declaration of God's absolute perfection and transcendence
key_terms.عَرَفْتَ: Recognized/knew (ma'rifa) — intimate knowledge of God through God's own self-disclosure
key_terms.عَرَّفَنِي نَفْسَهُ: He introduced Himself to me — divine self-disclosure (ta'rif) as the basis of all gnosis
key_terms.قَرِيبٌ فِي بُعْدِهِ بَعِيدٌ فِي قُرْبِه: Near in His remoteness, Remote in His nearness — divine paradox transcending spatial categories
key_terms.لَا يُشْبِهُهُ صُورَةٌ: No image resembles Him — tanzih (transcendence/incomparability), the core Shia theological principle
key_terms.مُبْتَدَأٌ: Initiator/Originator — God as the First Cause, the one who initiates all things

ai.seo_question: How did Imam Ali describe the knowledge of God and His transcendent attributes?
ai.summary: In this celebrated dialogue, Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (AS) articulates a profound apophatic theology — he describes God through what God is not and through paradoxes that transcend human categories. When asked how he recognized his Lord, the Imam first declares that God Himself initiated this recognition, then proceeds to describe God's absolute transcendence: God cannot be imaged, sensed, or compared to humans. The seemingly contradictory pairs — near yet remote, above yet with nothing above, inside yet not like contained things, outside yet not like separated things — are not logical contradictions but rather expressions of God's unique mode of existence that defies spatial and categorical limitation. The hadith was transmitted through Ali ibn Uqba, a companion descended from a freed slave of the Prophet, reflecting the early community's diverse social composition.
